days.note: Park at Alpental and be scrambling the talus cone by first light, aiming to start the roped climbing within an hour of leaving the car. Published reports range from about 8 hours for a fast, competent pair to 14+ hours for a party that pitches everything out; one well-known report started at 10:30 am and exited at 1 am.

The direct line is about 6.2 miles round trip with roughly 6,000 ft of gain; that party's Gorge Creek/South Buttress line with detours ran 10 miles and about 7,400 ft.

days.note: This is a big single-day outing, not a backpack. days.note: Take the Snow Lake trail and the Source Lake fork, then cross talus and climb the steep gully toward Pineapple Pass. days.note: Leave the Blue Lake trail at about 1.5 mi and take the climbers' path into the basin; Steph Abegg reports a little over an hour from the car and North Cascades Mountain Guides say about 1.5 hours. Descend the six-station bolted rappel line about 15 ft right of the finish with a 70 m rope, or take the original rappels via the notch and chockstone; either takes about 40 minutes back to the packs. Gain is derived from the row's elevations; miles are an estimate.

itinerary.cal: NPS backcountry permit required in North Cascades National Park for overnight stays — $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, reserved on Recreation.gov; best climbed July-August when the couloir holds consolidated neve rather than bare/rotten ice.

days.note: From the climbers' boot path off the Mt Baker Highway, hike Ruth Creek/Price Lake trail through steep forest, cross the Nooksack's North Fork on a large log, then grind up moraine above Price Lake to a ridge goat-path that leads to a flat rock bivy site (room for 2-3 bivies) overlooking the Price and East Nooksack Glaciers. Expect brush, an exposed log crossing, and real route-finding; most parties reach camp by mid-afternoon.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach the 5,900 ft bivy camp on the ridge above Price Lake

days.note: This is the crux day and it is very long: an 800 ft, 50-60 degree (one 70 degree step) snow/ice couloir off the bergschrund leads into loose rock, then roughly 10 pitches of exposed class 4-5 climbing along the arete to the summit. The descent reverses the route with about ten 60m rappels plus downclimbing, often finishing in the dark; strong parties are back at camp 15-17 hours after leaving.

days.note: Reverse the approach: goat-path off the ridge, down the moraine past Price Lake, steep forest, and the log crossing back to the trailhead. Legs are tired and the log crossing/brush demand care on tired legs, but it's straightforward compared to the day before.

itinerary.cal: Best as a spring-to-early-summer snow climb (roughly April through June) while the glacier and couloir hold good snow and the bergschrund is filled in. Usually done in two days with a camp in the basin; an Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is needed from May 15 to October 31, and very fit parties do it car to car.

days.note: Follow the Stuart Lake trail past the Colchuck junction, then leave it and work up the south fork of Mountaineer Creek (route-finding is tricky; expect boulder fields and creek crossings) to the flat basin at about 5,400 ft. Gain is derived from the trailhead (3,400 ft) and camp (5,400 ft) elevations.
days.title: Hike in to the Mountaineer Creek basin
days.objective: Camp in the basin below the Sherpa Glacier

days.note: Climb the Sherpa Glacier to the col at about 8,300-8,600 ft (the schrund is usually passed on climber's right in spring), then follow the southeast ridge to the summit. Descend the same glacier back to camp (best early season), pack up and walk out; gain and loss derived from camp (5,400 ft) to summit (9,415 ft) to trailhead (3,400 ft).
days.title: Climb the Sherpa Glacier and hike out
days.objective: Summit Mount Stuart and return to the car

itinerary.totalNote: The classic two-day plan: walk in to a camp in the Mountaineer Creek basin at about 5,400 ft, then climb the Sherpa Glacier to the summit and descend the same way before hiking out, roughly 6,000 ft and 16 miles round trip.

itinerary.cal: Best attempted in late summer (Aug-Sep) once the glacier crossing between Tin Can Gap and the Middle/North col is more consolidated and less crevassed; carry a rope, rack, and glacier gear in addition to standard scrambling kit.

days.note: Walk or bike the 8 closed miles of FR 41 from the Canyon Creek bridge to Tupso Pass first. Same approach as the standard South Peak trip: Saddle Lake Trailhead through old-growth forest and Saddle Lake up to the meadows at Goat Flats. Carry the technical rack and glacier gear in addition to overnight kit since North Peak's harder climbing is ahead.

days.note: From camp, cross Tin Can Gap and drop roughly 400 ft onto the Queest-Alb Glacier before climbing back up about 1,000 ft to the col between Middle and North Peak. Rope up for sustained class 4 climbing with one low-5th-class (5.1) move in a summit chimney; exposure is constant.
